title: Foreign Investors Have Pulled ₹2.87 Lakh Crore From India as AI Trade Reshapes Global Flows
excerpt: Premium valuations, the global AI-chip rotation into Korea and Taiwan, and geopolitical risk have driven the sharpest FPI exodus in years — but domestic institutions are absorbing every rupee.
body:
• Foreign portfolio investors withdrew ₹2.87 lakh crore from Indian equities by mid-June 2026, after pulling ₹1.66 lakh crore in all of CY2025
  • AI-linked capital rotation to South Korea and Taiwan, India's premium Nifty PE of 21-22x, and geopolitical tensions are the primary drivers
  • Domestic institutional investors have fully absorbed the selling, powered by record mutual fund SIP inflows
  • Foreign ownership of Indian equities has dropped from ~20% to ~15% over the past decade

Foreign portfolio investors have pulled a staggering ₹2.87 lakh crore from Indian equities by mid-June 2026, according to depository data, accelerating a retreat that has fundamentally altered who owns India's stock market. The outflows dwarf the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of calendar year 2025, with ₹1.92 lakh crore leaving in just the first four months of 2026.

Why Foreign Money Is Leaving

Three forces are converging. First, the global AI trade has redirected billions into semiconductor-heavy markets. South Korea (Samsung, SK Hynix) and Taiwan (TSMC) have become the primary beneficiaries as institutional investors chase the AI hardware supply chain. India, with limited exposure to chip manufacturing, has been a funding source for those bets.

Second, Indian valuations remain steep. The Nifty 50 trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 21-22x, a premium to most emerging market peers. For global allocators benchmarking returns against cheaper markets, the math has been difficult to justify, especially with earnings growth moderating.

Third, intermittent geopolitical tensions — from border dynamics with China to global trade policy uncertainty — have kept risk premiums elevated for India-focused foreign capital.

"India has become a funding market. The days of depending on foreign money are behind us."

— Raamdeo Agrawal, Chairman, Motilal Oswal Financial Services

The Domestic Backstop

What makes this cycle different from previous FPI exits is the sheer scale of domestic absorption. Indian mutual funds, fueled by record systematic investment plan (SIP) inflows that now exceed ₹25,000 crore per month, have stepped in as the market's primary buyer. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) have matched FPI selling almost rupee for rupee, preventing the kind of sharp drawdowns that accompanied foreign exits in 2018 or 2020.

The structural shift is dramatic. Foreign ownership of Indian listed equities has declined from roughly 20% a decade ago to about 15% today, even as total market capitalisation has more than tripled. Indian households, channeling savings through mutual funds and insurance products, now hold a larger share of the market than at any point in modern history.

What It Means for Investors

For NRI investors with India exposure, the FPI exodus creates a paradox. Markets have held up despite the selling, suggesting underlying demand is robust. But the valuation premium that drove foreigners out remains, meaning near-term returns may be compressed compared to cheaper emerging markets.

Fund managers say the real risk is not the FPI outflow itself but what happens if domestic flows slow. SIP growth has been linear for years, but a sustained market correction could test retail investor resolve. For now, India's equity market has effectively decoupled from foreign capital dependency — a structural shift that will shape return expectations for years to come.
